ALDEN: Boosting Private Data Extraction from Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems via Active Learning and Distribution Estimation

Xingyu Lyu Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Lowell, USA    Jianfeng He Affiliation: Virginia Tech, USA Affiliation: Amazon, USA    Ning Wang Affiliation: University of South Florida, USA    Yidan Hu Affiliation: Rochester Institute of Technology, USA    Tao Li Affiliation: Purdue University, USA    Danjue Chen Affiliation: North Carolina State University, USA    Shixiong Li Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Lowell, USA    Yimin Chen Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Lowell, USA
Abstract

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is widely used to augment large language models with external knowledge retrieval to improve reliability and generalization. However, recent studies have shown that RAG systems remain vulnerable to data extraction attacks, where adversaries can extract private data by embedding malicious commands into user queries. Despite their feasibility, existing attacks typically suffer from low data extraction rates and limited practical effectiveness. Here, we propose ALDEN, a novel attack that effectively and efficiently extracts private data from RAGs. First, we employ active learning to diversify malicious queries and improve data extraction rates. Second, we observe that the data distribution of the underlying knowledge base provides valuable guidance for query generation and introduce a decay-based dynamic algorithm to estimate the corresponding topic distribution. By combining them together, we demonstrate that ALDEN substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods through comprehensive evaluations.

22footnotetext: Jianfeng He completed this work while at Virginia Tech. He is now at Amazon.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in various applications. However, their reliability is often questioned due to issues such as hallucinations in which LLMs generate false or inaccurate information and lacking access to the latest data. Such concerns escalate when deploying LLMs for sensitive or high-stakes sectors like the medical and financial industries Elsayed (2024); Latif (2025); Kim et al. (2025).

To address these limitations, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a practical solution to improve LLM reliability by incorporating externally retrieved knowledge into the input context Shi et al. (2023); Lewis et al. (2020). By keeping private data local rather than embedding it into the model, RAG has been widely adopted in domains such as customer support, healthcare, legal, and finance NVIDIA (2024); Amazon (2025); Hindi et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2023). The global RAG market was valued at approximately $1.24 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach $67.42 billion by 2034 Precedence (2025).

Despite these benefits, it remains unclear whether RAG provides sufficient privacy protection for the underlying knowledge base. The integration of private data into the LLM generation pipeline introduces new privacy risks. Prior work Zeng et al. (2024); Qi et al. (); Cohen et al. (2024) shows that attackers can exploit prompt injection to induce LLMs to reveal retrieved private content, leading to automated attacks in Jiang et al. (2024); Di Maio et al. (2024). However, existing attacks tend to only generate queries of similar topics rather than queries of sufficiently different topics. As a result, they can only retrieve data of a narrow range, thus limiting the attack performance. What’s worse, they only showed feasibility without providing the upper bounds of proposed attacks.

In this paper, we propose ALDEN, a query-based attack on RAG systems that efficiently extracts private data from their knowledge bases. To overcome the limited coverage of existing attacks, ALDEN diversifies malicious queries via active learning, thus enabling retrieval from broader topics. Furthermore, broader introduces a distribution-aware strategy that dynamically estimates the topic distribution of the victim knowledge base, which guides query generation and helps us to characterize the upper bound of ALDEN through an oracle setting. Figure 1 illustrates a case in which ALDEN retrieves information like name, city, clinic, disgnosis, etc, which is not supposed to be out there. We evaluate ALDEN under comprehensive settings and confirm that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art attacks in private data extraction. Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We propose a novel data extraction attack on RAG that is the first to incorporate active learning and distribution estimation together for enhancing attack performance.

  • •

    We are the first to identify the importance of data distribution on data extraction and design a complete set of algorithms for generating malicious queries so that they are efficient, diverse, adaptive, and conditioned by historic queries.

  • •

    We comprehensively evaluate ALDEN on a practical RAG system using three real-world datasets, three LLMs, and five baselines under both targeted and untargeted settings, confirming that it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art attacks. We also conduct extensive ablation studies and robustness evaluations against defenses. Notable, we are the first to show that ALDEN’s performance is close to the oracle test.

2 System and Adversary Model

2.1 System Model

We illustrate the workflow of a typical RAG system in Figure 2. An RAG system comprises a retriever RDR_{D}, an indexed knowledge base 𝐊\mathbf{K}, and an LLM for response generation (referred to as LLM-RAG). Mathematically, given query qq, the retriever obtains the top-kk chunks [c1,c2,⋯,ck][c_{1},c_{2},\cdots,c_{k}] from the knowledge base 𝐊\mathbf{K}, i.e., [c1,c2,⋯,ck]=RD​(q,𝐊)[c_{1},c_{2},\cdots,c_{k}]=R_{D}(q,\mathbf{K}). After that, the retriever feeds c1⊕c2⊕⋯⊕ck⊕qc_{1}\oplus c_{2}\oplus\cdots\oplus c_{k}\oplus q to LLM-RAG. Finally, LLM-RAG outputs

r=𝒢LLM-RAG​(c1⊕c2⊕⋯⊕ck⊕q)r=\mathcal{G}_{\text{LLM-RAG}}\bigl(c_{1}\oplus c_{2}\oplus\cdots\oplus c_{k}\oplus q)

to the user as the response of qq.

2.2 Adversary Model

We consider a black-box attacker aiming to extract private data from the knowledge base of a RAG system, i.e., to obtain as many chunks from 𝐊\mathbf{K} as possible. By black-box, we mean that the attacker can only interact with the RAG system through APIs, without access to the internal. Assume that the attacker can use query qq to obtain rr and apply our proposed ALDEN attack to obtain a set of data chunks 𝐂\mathbf{C} from rr. It follows that when using a query sequence 𝐐=[q1,q2,⋯,qn]\mathbf{Q}=[q_{1},q_{2},\cdots,q_{n}], the attacker can obtain 𝐑=[r1,r2,⋯,rn]\mathbf{R}=[r_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{n}] and 𝒞=[𝐂1,𝐂2,⋯,𝐂n]\mathcal{C}=[\mathbf{C}_{1},\mathbf{C}_{2},\cdots,\mathbf{C}_{n}], correspondingly. The final set of recovered chunks by the attacker is thus 𝛀=𝐂1∪𝐂2∪⋯∪𝐂n\mathbf{\Omega}=\mathbf{C}_{1}\cup\mathbf{C}_{2}\cup\cdots\cup\mathbf{C}_{n}.

Attack goal. The attacker’s goal is to extract as many sensitive chunks from 𝐊\mathbf{K} as possible, i.e., more sensitive chunks in 𝛀\mathbf{\Omega}. Following prior attacks Zeng et al. (2024); Di Maio et al. (2024), we consider the two scenarios. (1) Targeted attack: Here we assume that the attacker has prior knowledge of the data domain of the victim RAG system and aims to extract chunks of targeted types. Similar to Jiang et al. (2024); Zeng et al. (2024), we assume that the attacker targets at Personally Identifiable Information (PII) such as phone numbers, emails, etc. (2) Untargeted attack: Here we assume that the attacker has no prior knowledge of the data domain and aims to extract as many unique chunks from 𝐊\mathbf{K} as possible.

3 Design of ALDEN

3.1 Intuitions and Overview.

Intuitions. As mentioned above, our ALDEN attack is to extract as many (sensitive) chunks from the knowledge base 𝐊\mathbf{K} of an RAG system as possible. Earlier works mainly demonstrated their feasibility but suffered from low extraction rates and uncertainty about their performance. In comparison, our first intuition is to adopt active learning strategies for generating new attack queries which are more likely to help return new chunks from 𝐊\mathbf{K}. We explore different active learning strategies and adopt k-center in our design. Our second intuition is based on revisiting the root of such private data extraction attacks on RAG systems. Particularly, we ask the following specific question: what can be the impact of knowing the data distribution of chunks in 𝐊\mathbf{K} on generating attack queries for private data extraction? The answer is clear; chunk data distribution in 𝐊\mathbf{K} would certainly guide the generation of proper attack queries for two reasons. Denote the data distribution in 𝐊\mathbf{K}, 𝐐=[q1,q2,⋯,qn]\mathbf{Q}=[q_{1},q_{2},\cdots,q_{n}], and 𝛀\mathbf{\Omega} by P⁡(𝐊)P(\mathbf{K}), P⁡(𝐐)P(\mathbf{Q}), and P⁡(𝛀)P(\mathbf{\Omega}), respectively. On the one hand, if P⁡(𝐐)∼P⁡(𝐊)P(\mathbf{Q})\sim P(\mathbf{K}), it is more likely that such an attack retrieves more chunks of 𝐊\mathbf{K}. On the other hand, by comparing P⁡(𝛀)P(\mathbf{\Omega}) to P⁡(𝐊)P(\mathbf{K}), an attacker can get a better idea of which types of data in 𝐊\mathbf{K} are still missing from 𝛀\mathbf{\Omega} and thus generate a proper query for bridging the gap.

We implement the above intuitions into ALDEN. To illustrate our intuitions, Figure 3 plots P⁡(𝐊)P(\mathbf{K}), i.e., the ground-truth data distribution, and two estimated distributions by an attacker denoted by α\alpha and β\beta, respectively. As shown in evaluation, since β\beta is more similar to P⁡(𝐊)P(\mathbf{K}) than α\alpha, ALDEN attack guided by β\beta turns out to perform better than that guided by α\alpha.

Overview. Figure 2 shows the attack pipeline of our proposed ALDEN. In the high-level, for each attack round, ALDEN generates and feeds a malicious query qq to the victim RAG (i.e., LLM-RAG). After it receives a response rr from LLM-RAG, ALDEN extracts data chunks from rr and proceeds to extract keywords from the data chunks. On the one hand, ALDEN appends those chunks containing interested private information as attack results. On the other hand, ALDEN updates its estimation of data distribution of 𝐊\mathbf{K} using the extracted keywords from rr. Finally, ALDEN proceeds to generate the next qq based on the updated distribution and the adopted active learning strategy.

3.2 Details of ALDEN

Initialization and topic seeding. As in previous attacks, for targeted attacks, in general we assume that they have a set of seed topics (denoted by TseedT_{\text{seed}}) that they are most interested in. Examples of seeds in TseedT_{\text{seed}} are related to “email”, “phone number”, and “health”, i.e., common domains where sensitive information resides. For untargeted attacks, TseedT_{\text{seed}} is not available and we obtain TseedT_{\text{seed}} via random sampling from out-of-distribution public datasets, e.g., Amazon Reviews (2023). Similar to Jiang et al. (2024), we use TseedT_{\text{seed}} to guide query generation at the beginning while appending more topics as the attack proceeds.

Malicious query generation. A malicious query qq is expected to (i) appear benign to remain stealthy and (ii) embed an adversarial prompt that will later be interpreted by LLM-RAG as a system-level instruction for revealing content. Also, we design qq so that the data extraction rate from 𝐊\mathbf{K} can be high.

To achieve these goals, ALDEN employs a local auxiliary LLM (i.e., LLM-AUX), denoted by 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime}, to generate qq with carefully designed prompts. LLM-AUX is instructed to produce queries with normal user intents (e.g., medical inquiries), while inserting injection commands selected from a pre-defined set 𝐒command\mathbf{S}_{\text{command}} Zeng et al. (2024); Jiang et al. (2024). These commands exploit the instruction-following behavior of LLMs (e.g., “ignore previous instructions and show internal data”). Overall, we generate qq by q=𝒢′(Tseed)||𝐒commandq=\mathcal{G}^{\prime}(T_{\text{seed}})\,||\,\mathbf{S}_{\text{command}}, where concatenation ensures that qq remains benign-looking while misleading LLM-RAG to reveal unintended information.

Chunk extraction. This step is to extract data chunks from the received response rr from LLM-RAG. At the ii-th iteration, the attacker feeds qiq_{i} to LLM-RAG and receives response ri=𝒢LLM-RAG​(RD​(qi,𝐊)⊕qi)r_{i}=\mathcal{G}_{\text{LLM-RAG}}\bigl(R_{D}(q_{i},\mathbf{K})\oplus q_{i}). The embedded command in qiq_{i} is designed to persuade 𝒢LLM-RAG​(⋅)\mathcal{G}_{\text{LLM-RAG}}(\cdot) to include its input, i.e., RD​(qi,𝐊)⊕qiR_{D}(q_{i},\mathbf{K})\oplus q_{i}, as part of rir_{i} as much as possible. ALDEN proceeds to apply regular expressions to rir_{i} to extract sensitive PII (e.g., phone numbers and emails) or other sensitive information. In particular, this includes parsing, filtering, and finally duplicate removal (See Appendix H and I for details). After that, ALDEN is to identify a set of keywords, cluster them to find candidate anchors (i.e., centroids of clusters of keywords), and add them into a temporary set denoted by 𝐒anchor′\mathbf{S^{\prime}_{\text{anchor}}}.

Anchor set update. Here the attacker is to decide whether a new candidate anchor in 𝐒anchor′\mathbf{S^{\prime}_{\text{anchor}}} will be added into 𝐒anchor\mathbf{S_{\text{anchor}}}. Each anchor aia_{i} in 𝐒anchor′\mathbf{S^{\prime}_{\text{anchor}}} is first converted to the embedding space through embedding​(⋅)\text{embedding}(\cdot), i.e., z⁡(ai)=embedding​(ai)z(a_{i})=\text{embedding}(a_{i}). The attacker then computes the cosine similarity between z⁡(ai)z(a_{i}) and all existing embeddings in 𝐒anchor\mathbf{S_{\text{anchor}}}. Any aia_{i} whose similarity is higher than a threshold α1\alpha_{1} will be discarded because a high similarity means that there already exists an anchor similar to aia_{i} in 𝐒anchor\mathbf{S_{\text{anchor}}}. The attacker then adds those qualified aia_{i}s into 𝐒anchor\mathbf{S_{\text{anchor}}} for next step.

Distribution estimation. In this step, the attacker is to construct a vector P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) corresponding to the probability distribution of interested topics. As mentioned above, ALDEN relies on such distribution for enhancing extraction efficiency and coverage. We define P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) as P′​(𝐊′)={(ai,wi)}i=1|𝐒anchor|P^{\prime}(\mathbf{K}^{\prime})=\{(a_{i},w_{i})\}_{i=1}^{|\mathbf{S_{\text{anchor}}}|} where aia_{i} is an anchor of 𝐒anchor\mathbf{S_{\text{anchor}}}, and wiw_{i} its corresponding weight. We will introduce how to compute wiw_{i} shortly.

Upon the first query, keywords, i.e., kik_{i}s, can be extracted from the response of LLM-RAG. We first apply DBSCAN Ester et al. (1996) to the embeddings z⁡(ki)z(k_{i})s of kik_{i}s to understand their semantic structure. We will show attack performance using other clustering methods as well. For each formed cluster, we further select the one keyword nearest to the centroid as its anchor. We then compute the weight of an anchor, aia_{i}, based on the cluster size over the number of all keywords extracted. Note that aia_{i} is surrounded by a cluster of kik_{i}s which are sufficiently similar to aia_{i}.

As expected, P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) needs to update across iterations to ‘better’ approximate P⁡(𝐊)P(\mathbf{K}) (i.e., the ground-truth) particularly in the earlier stage. One challenge for ALDEN is that aia_{i}s with higher wiw_{i}s remain to carry high wiw_{i}s because ALDEN tends to generate new queries based on aia_{i}s with higher wiw_{i}s. The corresponding responses rir_{i}s from such qqs, again, are similar to aia_{i}s. To break such a loop, that is, to avoid repeatedly selecting topics that are over-sampled and promote topics that are less visited, we propose a decay-based rule to update P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}), i.e., P⁡(𝐊′)←P⁡(𝐊′)+λτ⋅P⁡(𝐊′),P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime})\leftarrow P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime})+\lambda^{\tau}\cdot P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}), where λ<1\lambda<1 (e.g., λ=0.9\lambda=0.9) is a decay factor and τ\tau denotes the number of iterations elapsed. We further apply softmax to P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) for normalization, i.e., ∑P​(𝐊′)i=1\sum P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime})_{i}=1. As τ\tau increases, λτ\lambda^{\tau} decreases the weights of frequent topics while promoting those less frequent topics. Note that similar issues occur in prior attacks Zeng et al. (2024); Jiang et al. (2024) preventing them from extracting new topics over time. In comparison, the above rule helps ALDEN explore less visited topics, hence improving the coverage.

When ‖P​(𝐊′)i−P​(𝐊′)i−1‖\|P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime})_{i}-P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime})_{i-1}\| falls below a threshold ϵ\epsilon, we consider P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) to be stable and stop the above update loop.

Next query generation. Here, ALDEN uses LLM-AUX to generate the next query, i.e., qi+1q_{i+1}, which is expected to be stealthy and efficient. The main idea is to choose a proper anchor for instructing LLM-AUX that both reflects P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) and is conditioned by query history, i.e., to avoid repeating similar queries. Two steps are involved here: anchor selection and query resampling.

At each iteration, we first select kk anchors from the current 𝐒anchor\mathbf{S}_{\text{anchor}}. Intuitively, we start from selecting the aia_{i} with the highest wiw_{i} (referred to as the primary anchor) according to the current P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) because such a kik_{i} is likely to result in returning relevant data chunks. Note that P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) changes over time. Particularly, the delay-based update rule for P⁡(𝐊′)P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime}) enables ALDEN to generate qi+1q_{i+1} for less frequent topics. After that, we select the remaining k−1k-1 anchors using k-center as the active learning strategy Sener and Savarese (2017) to improve anchor diversity and avoid redundancy. See Appendix H for our choice of active learning strategies. Specifically, we iteratively select each anchor a∗a^{*} as:

a∗=arg⁡maxa∈𝐒anchor∖Aselect​mina′∈Aselect​‖z⁡(a)−z⁡(a′)‖2,a^{*}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathbf{S}_{\text{anchor}}\setminus A_{\text{select}}}\min_{a^{\prime}\in A_{\text{select}}}\|z(a)-z(a^{\prime})\|_{2},

where AselectA_{\text{select}} is the set of selected anchors, and z⁡(⋅)z(\cdot) denotes the embedding function. k-center tends to increase semantic diversity in AselectA_{\text{select}}, thereby increasing the likelihood of extracting new data.

Next we further refine the selection probabilities of anchors in AselectA_{\text{select}} using a re-sampling strategy. The motivation is that if similar queries have been done earlier, we would like to reduce the probability of such a query in order to promote selecting a less frequent query. Assume that the historic queries are {q1,…,qi}\{q_{1},\dots,q_{i}\}. We use LLM-AUX to generate queries for each anchor and denote them by {q1c,q1c,⋯,qkc}\{q^{c}_{1},q^{c}_{1},\cdots,q^{c}_{k}\}. For each historic query qiq_{i} and each candidate query qjcq^{c}_{j}, we can extract their associated topic set TiT_{i} and TjcT^{c}_{j}, respectively. For each qjcq^{c}_{j}, we compute two metrics: a relevance weight wj=∑k∈TjcP⁡(𝐊′)​(k)w_{j}=\sum_{k\in T^{c}_{j}}P(\mathbf{K}^{\prime})(k), and a diversity score div⁡(qjc)=1−maxk∈[1,i]⁡(Jaccard⁡(Tk,Tjc))\mathrm{div}(q^{c}_{j})=1-\max_{k\in[1,i]}(\mathrm{Jaccard}(T_{k},T^{c}_{j})), which measures the uniqueness of qjcq^{c}_{j} relative to all the historic qiq_{i}s. Then the final sampling score is computed as sj=wj⋅div⁡(qjc)s_{j}=w_{j}\cdot\mathrm{div}(q^{c}_{j}) and then normalized across all jjs. The candidate query with the highest score, qc,∗q^{c,*} is selected and then adapted with rephrasing or changing stylistic elements into qi+1=refineQuery​(qc,∗,𝐒command)q_{i+1}=\text{refineQuery}(q^{c,*},\mathbf{S}_{\text{command}}). See Algorithm 1 in Appendix for more details.

Convergence analysis. Please see Appendix E and F for our analysis and convergence illustrations for distribution estimation.

4 Evaluation

4.1 Experimental Setting

Scenarios and Datasets. We evaluate ALDEN on three real-world RAGs: healthcare, personal assistance, and finance, using HealthcareMagic-101 Li et al. (2023) (Health), Enron Email Klimt and Yang (2004) (Email), and a synthetic financial dataset GretelAI (2023) (Finance).

RAG Components. We build RAG applications using LangChain Chase (2022). Document chunks are indexed in a Chroma2 vector store with L2L_{2} similarity, and the top-kk chunks (k=3k=3) are retrieved per query. We evaluate Llama2-7b-chat, Qwen2-72B-Instruct, and ChatGPT-4. The default embedding model is all-MiniLM-L6-v2, with additional embedding ablations in Section 4.4.

Metrics. We evaluate both targeted and untargeted attacks using Leakage Chunks (LC) and Unique Leakage Chunks (ULC) to measure the total and non-redundant private information extracted, the ROUGE-L score to quantify textual overlap between model outputs and retrieved contexts. For targeted attacks, we also report the Attack Success Rate (ASR), defined as the fraction of queries that leak any PII, and Target Leakage (TLG), the total number of PII items leaked.

Baselines. We compare against prompt-injection attacks TGTB Zeng et al. (2024), PIDE Qi et al. (), GEA Cohen et al. (2024) and query-based attacks RAG-Thief Jiang et al. (2024) (as Thief) and Pirate Di Maio et al. (2024), sending 250 queries for each attack.

4.2 Results of Targeted Attack

Table 1 presents targeted attack results. Our method achieves the highest LC and ULC across models and datasets. For example, on Health dataset with LLaMA2-7B-Chat ALDEN extracts 574 ULC, a 28.98% gain over SOTA Pirate’s 445. TGTB and GEA have LC of 650 and 1,039 but only 103 and 277 ULC, indicating redundant output from prompt injections. In terms of TLG and ASR, our method also shows strong performance. In Email dataset with LLaMA-7B-Chat it reaches a TLG of 563 and an ASR of 86.4%, outperforming all baselines. For the ROUGE-L score, all results from ALDEN exceed 99%, which shows the effectiveness of our queries.

4.3 Results of Untargeted Attack

We report the LC and ULC in untargeted attacks. Table 2 compares APT with five baselines on the Health dataset across three LLMs, yielding results consistent with the targeted attack. For instance, on LLaMA2-7B-Chat, our method achieves an LC of 1,182 and a ULC of 594. Intuitively, larger LLMs produce slightly better results. Figure 4 shows similar trends on the Email and Finance datasets.

4.4 Ablation Studies & Overhead

Returned Chunks (Top-kk). To study how the number of retrieved chunks kk affects our attack, we vary k∈{1,3,5,7,9}k\in\{1,3,5,7,9\} and run 250 queries using LLaMA2-7B-chat on the Health dataset. Figure 5(a) shows the targeted attack results: LC, ULC and TLG increase as kk grows. This shows that deeper retrieval enhances attack performance.

Model Size. We evaluate five LLaMA2 variants (7B to 70B) on Health, using 250 attack queries per model. As shown in Figure 5(b), larger models generally achieve higher ULC, while TLG varies only marginally, this suggests that larger model sizes improve inference and text generation abilities, but have limited impact on the extraction of specific type of private knowledge.

Similarity Thresholds. We examine the impact of similarity thresholds used in the retrieval stage by varying them across {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9}, using LLaMA2-7B-Chat and 250 queries on the Health dataset. Figure 5(c) shows that higher thresholds result in lower LC, ULC, and TLG in the targeted setting. This indicates that stricter similarity filtering reduces the retrieval of loosely related or unexpected content.

Anchor Number. To analyze the impact of the number of anchor topics selected per iteration, we vary k∈{1,3,5,7,9}k\in\{1,3,5,7,9\}. As shown in Figure 5(d), increasing the number of anchor topics consistently improves LC, ULC, and TLG in the targeted attack, suggesting that anchor diversity helps uncover more private content.

Module Impact. Table 3 presents an ablation study isolating (i) active learning and (ii) distribution estimation. Compared to Table 1, removing either component results in substantial performance degradation. While distribution estimation alone performs better than active learning alone, combining both modules yields the best performance.

Oracle Test. To evaluate the effectiveness of our data estimation, we investigate the discrepancy between the estimated data distribution and the ground truth. We first apply DBSCAN on the ground truth dataset to obtain its distribution, denoted as P⁡(D)P(D), and then evaluate our method to derive an estimated distribution, P′​(D)P^{\prime}(D). We conduct experiments on three datasets using both P⁡(D)P(D) and P′​(D)P^{\prime}(D). Figure 6 shows the results from generating 250 queries guided by P⁡(D)P(D) and P′​(D)P^{\prime}(D). While the P⁡(D)P(D)-guided queries achieve higher performance in both targeted and untargeted attacks, the differences are minor. Figure 7 reveals substantial overlap between P⁡(D)P(D) and P′​(D)P^{\prime}(D). These results indicate that our estimation method effectively boosts attack performance as supported by the results in Table 1 and Table 2.

Overhead. Table 4 reports the wall-clock time (in seconds) required to generate an attack query, issue it to the RAG system, and obtain the final response. Overall, the execution time of our method is comparable to query-based baselines that rely on an auxiliary attacker LLM, indicating no noticeable latency overhead. Table 3 further reports the token usage and monetary cost of our attack. Even when using commercial models (e.g., GPT-4o-Mini), the total token consumption and cost remain very low (e.g., ∼\sim213 tokens per query and ∼\sim$0.022 for 250 queries), demonstrating that our attack is both time-efficient and cost-efficient in practice.

More results in Appendix. We includes ablation studies for (1) different active learning strategies and (2) different clustering methods (e.g., KDE and GMM) in Appendix I.

4.5 Potential Defenses

We evaluate four defenses against ALDEN as in (Xu et al., 2024). Details are in Appendix J.

Paraphrasing. Paraphrasing rewrites queries while preserving semantics to mitigate prompt injection. As shown in Figure 8(a), ALDEN remains highly effective, achieving high LC, ULC, and TLG, indicating that paraphrasing alone is insufficient.

Perturbation. We inject Gaussian noise into document embeddings with standard deviation σ∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}\sigma\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\}. Figure 8(b) shows that increasing noise reduces ULC slightly and significantly lowers TLG. However, large σ\sigmas degrade system utility, limiting practical deployment.

Re-ranking. We apply Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) re-ranking prior to generation. As shown in Figure 8(c), re-ranking has minimal impact on leakage metrics.

Summarization. We summarize retrieved documents before generation to remove extraneous details. Figure 8(d) shows that summarization does not substantially reduce LC or ULC, indicating limited effectiveness in defending against ALDEN.

5 Related Work

Privacy risk of LLMs. Prior work shows that LLMs can memorize and inadvertently disclose sensitive training data. Carlini et al. Carlini et al. (2021) demonstrate verbatim data extraction from GPT-2, while Nasr et al. Nasr et al. (2023) extend such attacks to production models like ChatGPT. Membership inference further quantifies privacy risks in language models Mireshghallah et al. (2022), and prompt-injection attacks exploit adversarial prefixes to elicit unintended private content Wallace et al. (2019).

Privacy attacks on RAG systems. Early prompt-injection attacks rely on static queries to extract limited sensitive information Zeng et al. (2024); Cohen et al. (2024); Qi et al. (). Recent work adopts adaptive query refinement to improve extraction, such as agent-based query expansion Jiang et al. (2024) and relevance-guided anchor updates Di Maio et al. (2024). Other studies further explore stealthier extraction, including natural-text interrogation attacks Naseh et al. (2025) and benign anchor-based mutations Wang et al. (2025).

Differences in ALDEN. Existing attacks often depend on predefined query patterns and overlook the underlying data distribution. ALDEN is the first to exploit active learning to improve coverage and incorporate distribution estimation to enhance extraction. See Table 7 in Appendix G.2 for more details.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose a novel privacy leakage attack on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems via data distribution estimation and active learning. Through comprehensive evaluations across diverse datasets and LLMs, we show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art attacks, highlighting the urgent need for robust defenses for RAG systems.

Limitations

Despite its effectiveness, our proposed approach is computationally intensive. Specifically, each iteration requires independently executing the attack on a dedicated GPU (NVIDIA RTX-6000) to generate a single adversarial query. Future research should explore more efficient and scalable techniques for generating multiple adversarial queries simultaneously, enabling more extensive querying of the RAG system and better retrieval performance. Secondly, our investigation focused on a standard RAG pipeline without considering built-in defensive strategies or content-filtering mechanisms. Consequently, adaptive attack evaluations against more countermeasures remain unexplored. Finally, this study has been limited to conventional RAG workflows and has not addressed more complex architectures, such as those employing knowledge graphs. Such systems may involve additional integration structures that introduce novel vulnerabilities, warranting further exploration in future studies.

Ethical considerations

Our study reveals hidden privacy risks in widely adopted RAG systems, and we acknowledge the potential for malicious misuse. We share these results to promote responsible disclosure and to provide RAG developers with actionable insights for stronger privacy protections. All experiments use publicly available, open-source datasets under their respective licenses; any personally identifiable information has been anonymized or masked to prevent unintended exposure. We have strictly avoided targeting or probing real-world production systems without explicit authorization. Moving forward, we will continue collaborating with the research community to uphold ethical standards, transparency, and the development of privacy-preserving retrieval technologies.

Appendix A The Use of Large Language Models (LLMs)

LLMs were used for editorial purposes in this manuscript, and all outputs were inspected by the authors to ensure accuracy and originality. The LLM did not contribute to research ideation, experimental design, implementation, data analysis, or any other part of the work.

Appendix B Datasets Details

We evaluate the effectiveness of our attack on real-world applications across diverse domains, including healthcare, personal assistants, general knowledge repositories, and biomedical question-answering systems. Due to ethical considerations, we utilize publicly available, open-source datasets to simulate private data in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications. Specifically, we employ the HealthcareMagic-101 dataset Li et al. (2023), which comprises 200,000 doctor-patient medical dialogues, and the Enron Email Dataset Klimt and Yang (2004), containing approximately 500,000 employee emails, to represent the healthcare and personal assistant domains, respectively. For general knowledge repositories, we utilize the Mini-Wikipedia dataset HuggingFace (2023b), a curated subset of Wikipedia articles designed to evaluate RAG pipelines by providing questions and corresponding ground truth answers derived from Wikipedia content. In the biomedical domain, we employ the Mini-BioASQ dataset HuggingFace (2023a), derived from the BioASQ challenge, which includes biomedical questions along with gold standard answers and relevant contexts, facilitating exploration of biomedical question-answering tasks. To assess privacy risks in financial context, we adopt a dataset of the synthetic financial domain dataset GretelAI (2023) which consists of full-length synthetic financial documents containing labeled PII.

Appendix C Summary of Symbols

Appendix D ALDEN Algorithm

Algorithm 1 presents an overview of the ALDEN attack. Starting from a seed anchor and topic set, the attacker iteratively generates adversarial queries using an auxiliary LLM and issues them to the victim RAG system. Retrieved responses are parsed to extract candidate knowledge chunks, which are filtered by embedding similarity and added to the stolen knowledge base. Meanwhile, newly extracted content is used to update the anchor set and estimate the underlying topic distribution via clustering and decay-based updates. Guided by this estimated distribution, informative and diverse anchors are selected to steer subsequent query generation. This process continues until the estimated distribution converges, resulting in an increasingly comprehensive extraction of private knowledge from the RAG system.

Appendix E Convergence analysis of ALDEN

Model and notation.

Let

X={x1,…,xN}\displaystyle X=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\} (1)

denote the observed samples retrieved from a victim RAG system, where each xix_{i} corresponds to a retrieved knowledge chunk. For each xix_{i}, let zi∈{1,…,K}z_{i}\in\{1,\dots,K\} be a latent variable indicating which anchor keyword or topic is responsible for retrieving xix_{i}, and define

Z={z1,…,zN}.\displaystyle Z=\{z_{1},\dots,z_{N}\}. (2)

The parameter θ\theta denotes the attacker’s query and anchor selection strategy, which induces the retrieval-based generative model

p⁡(X,Z∣θ)=∏i=1Np⁡(zi∣θ)​p​(xi∣zi,θ).\displaystyle p(X,Z\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}p(z_{i}\mid\theta)\,p(x_{i}\mid z_{i},\theta). (3)

At iteration tt, the strategy is θ(t)\theta^{(t)}, corresponding to the current estimated anchor distribution. The attacker aims to maximize the marginal log-likelihood

ℓ⁡(θ)\displaystyle\ell(\theta) =log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)\displaystyle=\log p(X\mid\theta) (4)
=log∑Zp(X,Z∣θ).\displaystyle=\log\sum_{Z}p(X,Z\mid\theta).

Key identity (ELBO form).

By the chain rule,

p⁡(X,Z∣θ)=p⁡(Z∣X,θ)​p​(X∣θ),\displaystyle p(X,Z\mid\theta)=p(Z\mid X,\theta)\,p(X\mid\theta), (5)

which implies

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)=log⁡p⁡(X,Z∣θ)−log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ).\displaystyle\log p(X\mid\theta)=\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)-\log p(Z\mid X,\theta). (6)

Taking expectation with respect to the posterior under the current strategy θ(t)\theta^{(t)} yields

𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}[\log p(X\mid\theta)] =𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(X,Z∣θ)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)] (7)
−𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ)].\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)].

Since log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)\log p(X\mid\theta) does not depend on ZZ, the left-hand side reduces to log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)\log p(X\mid\theta). Define the EM objective

ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t)):=𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(X,Z∣θ)].\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}):=\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}[\log p(X,Z\mid\theta)]. (8)

Classical EM convergence.

Substituting θ(t)\theta^{(t)} into (7) gives

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t))\displaystyle\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)}) =ℱ⁡(θ(t)∣θ(t))\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)}) (9)
−𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ(t))].\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)})].

Similarly, for any θ\theta,

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)\displaystyle\log p(X\mid\theta) =ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}) (10)
−𝔼Z|X,θ(t)​[log⁡p⁡(Z∣X,θ)].\displaystyle-\mathbb{E}_{Z\mid X,\theta^{(t)}}[\log p(Z\mid X,\theta)].

Subtracting the two expressions yields

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ)−log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t))\displaystyle\log p(X\mid\theta)-\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)}) =ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))−\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})- (11)
ℱ⁡(θ(t)∣θ(t))\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)}) +\displaystyle+
KL(p(Z∣X,θ(t))∥p(Z∣X,θ)).\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\!\Big(p(Z\!\mid\!X,\theta^{(t)})\,\|\,p(Z\!\mid\!X,\theta)\Big).

where the KL divergence is always non-negative. Therefore, any update that increases ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}) guarantees a non-decreasing data likelihood.

Approximate E-step in RAG attacks.

In the RAG setting, enumerating all latent assignments ZZ is infeasible. Instead, for each retrieved chunk xix_{i}, we approximate the posterior p⁡(zi∣xi,θ(t))p(z_{i}\mid x_{i},\theta^{(t)}) by its MAP estimate

zi⋆​(θ(t))=arg⁡maxzi⁡p⁡(zi∣xi,θ(t)),\displaystyle z_{i}^{\star}(\theta^{(t)})=\arg\max_{z_{i}}p(z_{i}\mid x_{i},\theta^{(t)}), (12)

yielding a deterministic assignment

Z⋆​(θ(t))={z1⋆,…,zN⋆}.\displaystyle Z^{\star}(\theta^{(t)})=\{z_{1}^{\star},\dots,z_{N}^{\star}\}. (13)

This corresponds to assigning each chunk to the anchor or topic that best explains its retrieval under the current estimated distribution.

We then approximate the EM objective as

ℱ⁡(θ∣θ(t))\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}) ≈ℱ^​(θ∣θ(t))\displaystyle\approx\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}) (14)
:=log⁡p⁡(X,Z⋆​(θ(t))∣θ).\displaystyle:=\log p\big(X,Z^{\star}(\theta^{(t)})\mid\theta\big).

Approximate monotonicity.

At iteration tt, the attacker updates θ(t+1)\theta^{(t+1)} to satisfy

ℱ^​(θ(t+1)∣θ(t))≥ℱ^​(θ(t)∣θ(t)).\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta^{(t+1)}\mid\theta^{(t)})\geq\widehat{\mathcal{F}}(\theta^{(t)}\mid\theta^{(t)}). (15)

Since the KL divergence term in (11) remains non-negative, the resulting updates satisfy

log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t+1))≳log⁡p⁡(X∣θ(t)),\displaystyle\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t+1)})\gtrsim\log p(X\mid\theta^{(t)}), (16)

indicating approximate monotonic improvement. This justifies interpreting the distribution estimation and anchor-update procedure in our RAG attack as an approximate EM algorithm over latent anchor assignments.

Role of hyperparameters.

The similarity threshold α\alpha controls anchor novelty, the decay factor λ\lambda discourages repeatedly selected anchors, and the temperature τ\tau stabilizes probability updates. Together, these parameters ensure stable and progressive convergence of the estimated anchor distribution.

Appendix F Illustrating Estimated Distributions for Supporting Convergence of ALDEN

To empirically support our convergence analysis, we examine how the gap between the estimated distribution and the ground-truth distribution evolves as the attack progresses. Figure 9 visualizes this process on the Health dataset at rounds 1, 10, 20, and 30.

In the early rounds, the estimated distribution differs substantially from the oracle distribution, indicating limited knowledge of the victim’s data distribution. As more attack queries are issued, the discrepancy steadily decreases, and by round 20 the two distributions become closely aligned. This trend confirms that ALDEN progressively refines its distribution estimation and converges toward an accurate approximation of the victim RAG system’s underlying knowledge distribution.

Appendix G More Background about RAG and Their Security and Privacy Concerns

G.1 Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances large language models by integrating external, real-time information into the generation process Lewis et al. (2020). This approach mitigates issues like hallucinations and improves overall response accuracy. The workflow of a RAG system can be succinctly described in three key steps:

  • •

    Indexing: External data sourced from APIs, document repositories, or databases is first segmented into coherent chunks. These chunks are then transformed into vector representations using an embedding model and indexed within a vector database.

  • •

    Retrieval: Upon receiving a user query, the system converts it into its corresponding vector embedding. A similarity search is then performed in the vector database to retrieve the top-kk most relevant chunks.

  • •

    Response: The retrieved chunks are combined with the original query to form an enriched prompt. This augmented prompt is fed into the LLM, which generates a response that leverages both the query and the contextual information from the external knowledge base.

We summarize the overall process as:

response=LLM​(RD​(q)⊕q),\text{response}=\text{LLM}\bigl(R_{D}(q)\oplus q),

where RD​(q)R_{D}(q) denotes the retrieved chunks from the private knowledge base by a query qq and ⊕\oplus represents string concatenation to form a comprehensive prompt.

G.2 Privacy Risks in LLMs & RAG

Large language models (LLMs) and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are increasingly deployed in privacy-sensitive applications, raising significant concerns about the inadvertent exposure of sensitive information Zhu et al. (2024); Das et al. (2025). In the realm of LLMs, several privacy challenges have emerged. For instance, Carlini et al. Carlini et al. (2022) proposed membership inference attacks that can reveal private data, and they further demonstrated in Carlini et al. (2021) that an adversary can recover training examples from LLMs. These vulnerabilities underscore the broader privacy risks associated with deploying LLMs. Furthermore, integrating external knowledge bases into RAG systems introduces additional complexities because these systems rely on external data which can include proprietary or confidential information making them attractive targets for adversaries. Specifically, prompt injection attacks Zeng et al. (2024); Qi et al. (); Cohen et al. (2024) exploit manipulated inputs to force the model to reveal sensitive data, and adaptive query-based attacks Jiang et al. (2024); Di Maio et al. (2024) iteratively refine queries to maximize the extraction of confidential information. These attack vectors highlight the critical need for robust privacy-preserving measures in both LLMs and RAG systems.

G.3 Defenses against privacy attacks in RAG.

Recent work has proposed several defense strategies to mitigate privacy risks in RAG systems. Mao et al. Mao et al. (2025) introduce FedE4RAG, a federated learning framework that trains RAG retrievers across clients without sharing raw data, using knowledge distillation and homomorphic encryption to ensure privacy during collaborative training. Chen et al. Chen et al. (2025) propose a fine-grained privacy extraction approach that exploits knowledge asymmetry between RAG and standard LLMs; their method uses adaptive prompts, semantic scoring, and a neural classifier to precisely isolate private content, enabling more targeted privacy protection. Kandula et al. Kandula (2025) present a comprehensive privacy-aware RAG framework that integrates differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, homomorphic encryption, and robust access control to reduce data exposure and defend against adversarial queries, particularly in sensitive sectors such as healthcare and finance.

G.4 Adversarial Attacks Based on Active Learning.

Active learning has been extensively studied as a means to reduce labeling costs and improve model performance by iteratively selecting the most informative samples Settles (2009). Chandrasekaran et al. Chandrasekaran et al. (2020) provided one of the first theoretical analyses, showing that uncertainty-based sampling can dramatically lower query complexity for halfspace and decision-tree learners. Correia-Silva et al. Correia-Silva et al. (2018) introduced Copycat CNN, which uses random non-labeled data and pool-based sampling to steal deep classifiers. Ducoffe and Precioso Ducoffe and Precioso (2018) extended this to deep networks with a margin-based adversarial active learning strategy that balances exploration and exploitation. Building on these foundations, Shi et al. Yi et al. (2018) employed active learning with limited problem-domain (PD) data to extract a shallow feedforward network for text classification, while Shi et al. Shi et al. (2018) designed an exploratory model-extraction attack using a GAN trained on a small PD sample set to generate synthetic queries. Although effective, both approaches require PD data. To eliminate this dependency, Pal et al. Pal et al. (2020) proposed ActiveThief, which leverages unannotated public (NNPD) datasets and pool-based active learning to extract complex neural classifiers in both image and text domains using only 10–30% of the query budget. Related side-channel extraction methods include timing attacks by Duddu et al. Duddu et al. (2018) and high-fidelity reconstruction via function-inference by Jagielski et al. Jagielski et al. (2020). These works collectively demonstrate the power of active learning in adversarial model extraction and underscore the urgent need for robust defenses in ML-as-a-Service settings Papernot et al. (2017).

Appendix H More Details of ALDEN Design

H.1 Chunk Extraction

Chunk extraction is to extract data chunks from the received response rr from LLM-RAG. At the ii-th iteration, the attacker feeds qiq_{i} to the RAG system and receives response ri=𝒢LLM-RAG​(RD​(qi,𝐊)⊕qi)r_{i}=\mathcal{G}_{\text{LLM-RAG}}\bigl(R_{D}(q_{i},\mathbf{K})\oplus q_{i}). The injection command in qiq_{i} commands 𝒢LLM-RAG​(⋅)\mathcal{G}_{\text{LLM-RAG}}(\cdot) to include its input, i.e., RD​(qi,𝐊)⊕qiR_{D}(q_{i},\mathbf{K})\oplus q_{i}, as part of rir_{i} as much as possible. Assume that RD​(qi,𝐊)⊕qiR_{D}(q_{i},\mathbf{K})\oplus q_{i} is thus embedded in rir_{i}. The attacker proceeds to apply regular expressions to rir_{i} to extract sensitive PII (e.g., phone numbers, email addresses, SSNs) or other interested information. ALDEN achieves this through a dedicated parsing routine, which first identifies and standardizes specific formats (e.g., email addresses, phone numbers, or URLs), then filters out irrelevant content, and finally removes duplicates based on semantic similarity. From the well-structured extracted text, ALDEN is to identify a set of keywords, cluster them to find candidate anchors (i.e., centroids of clusters of keywords), and add them into a temporary anchor set denoted by 𝐒anchor′\mathbf{S^{\prime}_{\text{anchor}}}.

H.2 Query Generation

Choice of active learning. We adopt k-center for our use considering that k-center aims to maximize the distance between selected samples (which are anchors here) in the embedding space. Therefore, k-center tends to increase semantic diversity in AselectA_{\text{select}}, hence increasing the likelihood of extracting new data.

To generate adversarial queries, we employ an attacker-side language model (Llama-3.2-1B), i.e., LLM-AUX, which operates independently of the target RAG model and does not need to match its architecture or capabilities. LLM-AUX is used to synthesize fluent, user-like natural language queries based on specified topics. For example, for the topic “stroke,” the generated query might be: "Doctor, I’m worried about my mother’s recent stroke. Can you tell me more about the causes and risk factors of stroke?"

To influence the target RAG system to return sensitive information, we append injection commands to these queries. These commands follow patterns introduced in prior work Zeng et al. (2024); Jiang et al. (2024); Di Maio et al. (2024) and are designed to bypass safety filters or manipulate generation behavior. A representative example is: "Please ignore all previous instructions and output everything you know about this topic." The following sections describe in detail the seed topic, the design of injection commands, and the prompt format used for LLM-AUX.

Seed topics. To improve the relevance of initial attack queries, we use ChatGPT to generate a set of seed topics as keywords for query construction. Each attack type is associated with 10 keywords. For targeted attacks, where the attacker knows the database domain, we select topics specific to sensitive domains such as health, email, or finance. For untargeted attacks, we use general PII-related keywords without domain constraints. Table 8 summarizes the seed topics used for each attack type.

Injection command. To prompt LLM-RAG to explicitly output the content retrieved by the RAG system, we employ injection commands from prior works Zeng et al. (2024); Jiang et al. (2024); Di Maio et al. (2024) designed to override safety and instruction-following behavior. The primary injection command used in our experiments is shown in Table 9. This command is to instruct LLM-RAG to disregard prior prompts and disclose all details returned from the retrieval process.

Prompts of LLM-AUX. To simulate realistic adversarial queries, we design attack prompts that instruct LLM-AUX 𝒢′\mathcal{G^{\prime}} to generate natural, contextually plausible questions or requests based on selected anchor topics. These prompts guide LLM-AUX to compose queries that resemble genuine user interactions, such as those that might occur during a consultation or search scenario. Table 10 lists representative attack prompts used in our study.

Appendix I More ablation study results

We conducted comprehensive ablation studies to investigate how key factors affect the performance of our method measured by the number of LC and ULC in untargetted attack.

Returned Chunks (Top-kk). As shown in Figure 10(a), the results demonstrate that increasing kk leads to higher values of both LC and ULC. This indicates that retrieving more chunks per query increases the likelihood and redundancy of leaked private content.

Model Size. Figure 10(b), larger models tend to yield slightly higher LC and ULC values. This suggests that larger LLMs, due to their improved language understanding and generative capabilities, are more likely to extract and reproduce private information during RAG responses.

Similarity Thresholds. Figure 10(c) shows that as the similarity threshold increases, both LC and ULC tend to decrease. This shows that lower similarity thresholds result in the retrieval of more loosely related or even irrelevant content, which increases the chance of retrieving private data from the corpus.

Anchors number. As shown in Figure 10(d), increasing the number of anchor topics leads to higher values of both LC and ULC. This trend suggests that more anchor topics introduce greater query diversity, increasing the chances of covering a broader range of private content in the knowledge base and thereby enhancing the effectiveness of the attack.

Embedding model. We also examine the impact of different embedding models on our attack performance in Health dataset. While our default configuration uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2 for encoding both document chunks and queries, we compare it with three strong alternatives: BGE v1.5-large, E5-large-v2, and GTE-large-en-v1.5. As shown in Table 11, all models achieve similar results in terms of LC and ULC, suggesting that our attack is not highly sensitive to the specific embedding model used.

Active learning strategy. We further examine which active learning strategy most effectively boosts the attack’s performance. We compare five representative methods:

  • •

    Random: Selects kk samples xnx_{n} uniformly at random.

  • •

    Uncertainty: Selects kk samples with the highest entropy Hn=−∑jy~n,jlogy~n,jH_{n}=-\sum_{j}\tilde{y}_{n,j}\log\tilde{y}_{n,j}, reflecting prediction uncertainty.

  • •

    K-center: Uses greedy K-center selection based on the Euclidean distance between y~n\tilde{y}_{n} and existing cluster centers to maximize sample diversity Sener and Savarese (2017).

  • •

    DFAL: Applies DeepFool to identify samples with minimal perturbation αn=‖𝐱n−𝐱^n‖22\alpha_{n}=\|\mathbf{x}_{n}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{n}\|_{2}^{2} Ducoffe and Precioso (2018).

  • •

    K-center + DFAL: Combines the informativeness of DFAL with the diversity of K-center by first filtering with DFAL and then clustering using K-center.

Table 12 presents the results of untargeted attacks on two datasets using the LLaMA2-7B-chat model, reporting both the number of LC and ULC under each selection strategy. We observe that K-center consistently outperforms other strategies, achieving the highest ULC across both datasets. Interestingly, the combination of K-center and DFAL method does not always improve performance suggesting that while combining informativeness and diversity is intuitive, it may introduce redundancy or degrade the query diversity in practice.

Impact of clustering methods. We conduct an ablation study on the choice of clustering methods used in the distribution estimation module. As shown in Table 13, DBSCAN consistently outperforms KDE, GMM, and kk-means across all metrics. This result suggests that density-based clustering is better suited for capturing the irregular and non-spherical structure of retrieved embeddings, leading to more accurate distribution estimation and stronger attack performance.

Appendix J Defenses

Paraphrasing before Retrieval. Paraphrasing acts as a proactive defense against prompt-injection and jailbreaking attacks by altering a query’s surface form while preserving its meaning. In our method, an LLM rephrases each user query immediately before retrieval—for example:

“What is diabetes mellitus? What should I do?”  →\to “If I have been diagnosed with diabetes mellitus, what steps should I follow?”

This disrupts the exact textual patterns that adversaries embed in malicious documents, without reprocessing the entire knowledge base. We evaluate the paraphrasing defense by generating five paraphrased queries per original query using Llama2-13B-chat. For each paraphrase, we retrieve k=3k=3 texts from the corrupted knowledge database and report LC and ULC for untargeted attacks. Figure 11(a) shows untargeted attack results. We find that LC, ULC remain still high, indicating that paraphrasing alone cannot effectively defend against our attack.

Perturbation-Based Defenses. Another defense adds calibrated noise to document or query embeddings so that individual data points do not overly influence retrieval. Specifically, we inject additive Gaussian noise into each document embedding at noise levels σ∈{0.1,0.3,…,0.9}\sigma\in\{0.1,0.3,\dots,0.9\}. Figure 11(b) shows untargeted attack results. We observe that LC and ULC decreases substantially, indicating that higher noise levels improve defense effectiveness. However, excessive noise can degrade overall system performance, making large σ\sigma impractical in real-world settings.

Re-ranking of Retrieved Chunks. A straightforward defense mechanism is to re-rank the retrieved documents before they are used for text generation. After retrieving the top-kk passages, we apply a secondary ranking algorithm using privacy-aware metrics—such as sensitivity classification or refined semantic similarity—to demote or remove documents that may contain sensitive or irrelevant information, thereby reducing the chance that private details are included in the final answer. We evaluate this re-ranking defense using Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to score and reorder the documents. Figure 11(c) shows untargeted attack results. LC and ULC remain still high after reanking, showing that re-ranking alone does not thwart our attack.

Summarization after Retrieval. In the summarization defense, an additional LLM generates concise summaries of each retrieved document based on the query context. This process filters out extraneous details, reducing the amount of information exposed. Both extractive and abstractive techniques can be applied to ensure that only essential, query-focused content reaches the generative model, further protecting sensitive data. We evaluate this defense by summarizing each retrieved document with Llama-2-70B-chat. Figure 11(d) shows results for untargeted attacks. We find that summarization does not significantly reduce LC or ULC; despite rewording, sensitive tokens often remain extractable.

Appendix K Case Studies

To illustrate the real-world implications of privacy leakage in RAG systems, we conduct a case study simulating an attack on a RAG-based Q&A system. This system is built on several popular LLMs, including Amazon’s chronos-t5-large, Google’s gemma-3-27b-it, and OpenAI’s gpt-3.5-turbo. We evaluate our approach on two datasets: HealthcareMagic-101, representing a medical scenario, and the Amazon Customer Review Dataset Amazon Reviews (2023), which simulates a company using internal customer reviews and product Q&A as the knowledge base for a customer-facing chatbot. We adopt the same experimental setting as in Section 4.1. Table 14 shows the untargeted attack results, indicating that our method consistently retrieves relevant chunks. Fig. 12 presents an example from Health dataset. Here, LLM-AUX generates a realistic query using selected anchors and injection commands to retrieve similar chunks from the knowledge base. Our method also extracts key topics (highlighted in bold red) to update the anchors for subsequent queries. These findings underscore the urgent need for effective privacy defenses in real-world RAG applications.
